summary: Discusses a feature to support building greynets for both IPv4 and IPv6. It is an informational note rather than a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A greynet is a part of a network set up to watch what traffic arrives. This note talks about how to build one for both versions of IP.

subtitle: A sparsely populated network region to detect and trap unauthorized probes

tldr.problem: Traditional darknet intrusion detection systems require large blocks of unused IP addresses, which network operators cannot easily dedicate because they face pressure to use all allocated addresses. Additionally, once attackers learn what address ranges are darknet, they stop probing them.
tldr.mechanism: A greynet is a region of IP address space where unused addresses are scattered randomly within normal subnets, interspersed with active hosts. When traffic arrives for these unused addresses, routers can forward the traffic to security sensors.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can deploy intrusion detection on almost any network without dedicating large address blocks, and the random distribution of unused addresses makes it harder for attackers to identify and avoid the monitoring system.

facts.label: Deployment status
facts.value: Prototype tested; effective for both IPv4 and IPv6

facts.label: Key advantage
facts.value: Scattered unused addresses harder to detect than contiguous blocks

today: RFC 6018 is an Informational document that describes a network monitoring technique that combines practical feasibility with effective intrusion detection. While the concept has been successfully prototyped, it remains primarily of interest to large organizations and ISPs that need to detect unauthorized probing. Modern network defenders use greynets alongside other detection techniques like intrusion detection systems, firewall logs, and flow-based monitoring.

sections.title: Greynets and Network Monitoring
sections.content:
A greynet is a region of IP address space designed to detect unauthorized network scans and attack traffic. Unlike traditional darknets, which dedicate entire IP prefixes to monitoring, greynets scatter unused addresses throughout normal operational subnets. When a packet arrives for an unused address in a greynet, it reveals a likely security threat: either a network scanner probing for targets, a misconfigured system, or an attacker.

This RFC defines greynets for both IPv4 and IPv6, drawing on research from Harrop and others that demonstrated the concept's effectiveness. The approach solves a practical deployment problem: most network operators cannot afford to set aside entire address blocks for monitoring, and Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) pressure them to use allocated addresses productively.
sections.plainLanguage: A greynet is a way to catch intruders by leaving some fake phone booths in an office building. If someone tries to use a booth that should not exist, you know something is wrong.

sections.title: Traditional Darknets and Their Limitations
sections.content:
Organizations like CAIDA, University of Michigan, and Team Cymru have long used darknets (also called Network Telescopes) to monitor attack traffic. A darknet is a large contiguous block of IP addresses that are routed to a monitoring system but not actually assigned to any real hosts. Any traffic directed to darknet addresses is by definition suspicious.

However, darknets have two significant problems. First, once attackers discover which address ranges are darknet, they stop probing them, reducing the system's effectiveness. Second, network operators face increasing pressure to use their allocated address space productively rather than dedicate large blocks to monitoring. These constraints make traditional darknet deployment difficult in enterprise and smaller networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Darknets used to be like having an entire unused floor in a building to watch for intruders. But once thieves learn which floor is empty, they stop going there. Also, companies want to rent out every floor, not leave a big one empty.

sections.title: How Greynets Work
sections.content:
A greynet uses the natural unused address space that exists in most IP subnets. IPv4 subnets allocated by CIDR contain 2^n addresses, but most subnets use only a fraction of that space for actual hosts. Similarly, IPv6 subnets, by design, use only a small fraction of their 2^64 addresses. The key insight is that unused addresses in these subnets can serve as greynet sensors.

When a router receives a datagram for a destination address in its subnet, it uses Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) for IPv4 or Neighbor Discovery (ND) for IPv6 to learn the MAC address of that destination. If the address is a greynet address (unused), no response comes back. The router can detect this situation and forward a copy of the datagram to a collection system for analysis. This allows detection of scans targeting unused addresses within normal operational subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: Most network subnets have empty IP addresses because there are more addresses than actual computers. A greynet marks some of these empty addresses as monitoring points. When traffic arrives for an empty address, the router knows something suspicious happened.

sections.title: Deployment Approaches
sections.content:
Greynets can be deployed in two ways. The first approach uses routing: selecting specific prefixes that are advertised to the network but not actually deployed. For example, if a campus uses only odd-numbered subnets in its allocated space, the even-numbered subnets can be darknet prefixes, attracting all traffic to undeployed addresses. A collector system handles all this traffic.

The second approach uses sparse address space within active subnets. Individual unused addresses are scattered throughout normal subnets in a seemingly random pattern. This is more powerful because an attacker cannot distinguish between deployed and undeployed addresses by examining subnets. Detection occurs at routers when they attempt ARP or Neighbor Solicitation for these unused addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either block off entire empty floors for monitoring, or scatter fake office numbers throughout normal floors. The scattered approach is trickier to detect because intruders cannot tell which offices are real.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses several security implications. Forwarding traffic that triggers ARP or Neighbor Solicitation to a collector consumes some bandwidth and router resources, which attackers could potentially exploit through denial-of-service. However, router implementations can mitigate this by selecting only a subset of matching traffic to forward: only new events, only traffic above a certain rate, only unresponded requests, or only traffic matching specific filter rules.

For IPv4, the concept has been well-researched and prototyped. For IPv6, address scanning attacks have historically been rare due to the vast address space, but they are theoretically possible, especially if attackers can infer address ranges from other sources like DNS or application-layer information. Organizations can defend against this by using privacy addresses that periodically change, making historical address information less useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Monitoring everything at once could overwhelm the system, but the router can be smart and only report new or suspicious patterns. IPv6 is a huge space so scans are rare, but the concept still works there.
